verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster. A maskil of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster: a maskil, a song to teach the wise. Of David.
verses.directors_commentary: Verse 1 in the Hebrew is the superscription; the KJV prints it as unnumbered verse 0, so every KJV number in this psalm sits two behind the Hebrew. Treat the title as stage directions, not as scenery. 'To the choirmaster' means the psalm was handed to the temple choir, and 'maskil' suggests a piece meant to give insight, a song with a lesson in it. Ibn Ezra and Meiri both say the lesson is plain: the end of the wicked is evil. The KJV prints 'Maschil' untranslated and sets 'A Psalm of David' in the same line; the Hebrew title has no word for 'psalm' (mizmor) at all, only 'maskil', and 'of David' is a dedication or an authorship mark, as in other titles. Have the cast hear it as an instruction delivered by a man who has just survived, not as a lament.

philological_notes.note: Derived from sakhal, 'to be wise, to have insight'. It heads thirteen psalms and most likely names a skilful or didactic poem; Metzudat David reads it as a psalm in which David teaches the people to beware of slander (lashon hara).

verses.translation_literal: When Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, and said to him, "David has come to the house of Ahimelech."
verses.translation_dramatic: It began the day Doeg the Edomite walked into Saul's presence and spoke, and what he said was this, quietly, to the king: "David has come to the house of Ahimelech."
verses.directors_commentary: This is the second line of the superscription, and it tells the cast which night to remember. Doeg, an Edomite, one of Saul's herdsmen, was at Nob when David was fed by the priest; the story is 1 Samuel 21 and 22, and Ibn Ezra and Radak both say the psalm only abbreviates it because its audience knew it. Edomites were Israel's kin through Esau and its rivals, so an Edomite informing against an Israelite priest carries an edge that a modern reader misses. Notice how little Doeg says. Malbim reads the fragment as the whole offence: 'to the house of Ahimelech' makes the priest a host and a friend, where the truth was that David had come to the house of the LORD and to the priest only as priest. The KJV 'is come' smooths over a perfect that simply reports an arrival; the Hebrew has no 'house of the priest', and no motive for David. Play Doeg as flat, a clerk reporting an incident.

philological_notes.note: 'The Edomite', one who lived in Edom (Radak, Metzudat Zion), a descendant of Esau. In 1 Samuel 21:8 Doeg is Saul's chief herdsman.
The hiphil of nagad, 'to report, to tell up', the verb used for informing a superior. It is the same root that gives the later nominal sense of 'in front of' (neged, verse 11).

verses.translation_literal: Why do you boast in evil, O mighty man? The covenant loyalty of God [is] all the day.
verses.translation_dramatic: Why do you swagger, mighty man, and strut in your evil? The faithful love of God is here, every hour of the day.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens in the middle of a quarrel: David addresses Doeg directly, and the first word, 'why', is a taunt, not a request for information. 'Mighty man' (gibbor) is a title of a warrior or a man of standing, here used with a sting; Rashi, Metzudat David and the Talmud (Sanhedrin 106b) add that Doeg was mighty in Torah, so the irony is that a learned man chose evil. The verb tithallel is the one from which 'hallelujah' comes, so this is praise turned inside out: he boasts in the way others praise God. The KJV renders ra'ah as 'mischief', which is a weak word for a slander that ended in the killing of the priests of Nob; the Hebrew is the ordinary word for 'evil'. In the second line, 'chesed' is covenant loyalty, the reliable faithfulness of a God bound by promise, and the KJV 'goodness' (and 'endureth continually') adds a verb the Hebrew does not have: the sentence is only 'the chesed of God, all the day'. Give the second half a calm, almost dismissive delivery, set against the first half's heat.

philological_notes.note: Hithpael of halal, 'to praise oneself, to boast'; the same root as hallelu-Yah. Doeg offers himself the praise that belongs to God.
Covenant loyalty, steadfast love; Radak hears in it the many times God saved David from Saul. KJV 'goodness' is too generic.
'The mighty one', a vocative with the article (Meiri compares Numbers 15:15 and Jeremiah 2:31). Used ironically here.

verses.translation_literal: Ruin your tongue plots, like a sharpened razor, O doer of deceit.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your tongue is a workshop of ruin, hunched over its plans; it is a razor honed to a hair's edge, and you, you work the blade with a smile.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm now gives the tongue a mind of its own: it 'plots', and Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri all say this is because the tongue is the messenger of the heart, so that a thought becomes visible only when it is spoken. The key picture is the barber's razor (ta'ar, a knife that shaves; Metzudat Zion), and the point of 'deceit' is in Radak's reading: a man takes up a razor to cut a little and cuts a great deal, so a few words from Doeg meant eighty-five priests dead. Rashi and Metzudat David add that it cuts the flesh with the hair. The KJV 'deviseth mischiefs' is soft; hawwot is 'ruin, disaster', the same word used for the man's own end in verse 9, so what he plots against others returns on him. 'Working deceitfully' in the KJV turns a vocative noun phrase into an adverb; the Hebrew speaks to the doer ('O doer of deceit'), or perhaps to the razor itself. Have the actor speak the razor image slowly, as the sound of the blade on the strop.

philological_notes.note: Plural of hawwah, 'ruin, calamity, destruction' (Radak: 'a break and an evil matter, in deed or in thought'). Verse 9 uses the same noun for the man's own ruin.
A razor or knife used for shaving (Metzudat Zion); Rashi on the next phrase says it cuts flesh together with the hair.
Deceit, treachery. Ibn Ezra records an opinion that it comes from the root of mirmah (verse 6) and not from ramah, 'to throw', as in Exodus 15:1.

verses.translation_literal: You love evil more than good, falsehood more than speaking righteousness. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: You loved evil before you loved good; you loved a lie better than a true word. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: Doeg's offence is not an error. 'You love' is the verb of choice and desire, and the accusation (Meiri, Malbim, Ibn Ezra) is that he could have told the whole truth, that Ahimelech knew nothing of David's flight, and chose instead the version that would kill. The Hebrew compares with min: evil 'from' good, falsehood 'from' speaking righteousness, so the preference is placed before the audience like two bowls. The KJV 'lying' for sheker is a gerund the Hebrew does not use; it is the noun 'falsehood', set against a verb, 'speaking righteousness', which gives the line its lopsided shape. Selah is a pause or a musical lift, marked in the text, whose exact meaning no one has; Meiri says it means 'all your days you have done so', and the cast should simply hold the silence.

philological_notes.note: Comparative min: 'more than good'. Metzudat David reads it as 'rather than doing good'. Ibn Ezra notes that some read 'in place of', but he finds no precedent.
A liturgical or musical marker of unknown meaning; Meiri glosses it here as 'for all your days'. Left untranslated.

verses.translation_literal: You love all words of swallowing, a tongue of deceit.
verses.translation_dramatic: You love every word that swallows, every sentence that devours; you, tongue of deceit.
verses.directors_commentary: The verb is the same, 'you love', and the first word of verse 5 returns here as a drumbeat: the psalm repeats because it is accusing. 'Words of swallowing' (divrei vala') is a metaphor of a mouth that gulps down its victims. Ibn Ezra says the words will swallow Doeg himself, Meiri glosses them as 'words of destruction', and Metzudat David says they are slander spoken in a swallowed, secret murmur. The KJV 'devouring words' keeps the sense but not the strangeness of the Hebrew's bala', the noun of swallowing. The last phrase, 'a tongue of deceit', is usually taken as an address to Doeg, as the KJV does ('O thou deceitful tongue'), and it turns the man into his own organ; the tongue is his whole identity. Play the verse in a lower voice than the previous one: contempt, not anger.

philological_notes.note: The noun is from the verb 'to swallow' (cf. Numbers 16:30, the ground swallowing Korah). 'Words of swallowing' are words that consume and destroy (Meiri) or are murmured secretly (Metzudat David).
Deceit, treachery. Radak says the slander was made in deceit from the first day, for if Doeg had told Ahimelech how the king would see it, Ahimelech would have refused.

verses.translation_literal: Also God will tear you down to perpetuity; he will snatch you up and tear you away from [your] tent, and uproot you from the land of the living. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: And now God himself will pull you down, and for good; he will seize you and wrench you from your tent, and root you out of the land of the living. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: The tone turns from accusation to sentence. 'Also' (gam) marks the justice of it: as you tore down, so you will be torn down. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all say that Doeg destroyed the house of the priests and now God destroys his own; Ibn Ezra says Doeg will be done to as he did to Ahimelech's family. The Hebrew packs four verbs in a short line, each with its own image: a building pulled to pieces (natatz), a verb of seizing or breaking (chatah), a plant pulled up (nasach, as in Proverbs 15:25) and a root torn out (sherash). The second is the hard one. Lexically it is the rare root chatah, 'to snatch up'; Rashi glosses it as breaking, and Meiri reads it as 'break you', like 'lest I break you before them' (Jeremiah 1:17), and reports another opinion, 'burn you', like 'you heap coals upon his head' (Proverbs 25:22). The KJV 'destroy', 'take away', 'pluck out' and 'root out' keeps the order but blurs the first two. Two details matter to the cast. 'Tent' (ohel) is the home, but Malbim and Ibn Ezra hear the sanctuary tent, from which the Edomite, who had been 'detained before the LORD' at Nob, is now expelled. 'The land of the living' is an idiom for this world, in the plain sense; Radak adds that it may mean the world to come. Deliver it as a verdict read in court, not a curse.

philological_notes.note: 'He will tear you down': the verb for demolishing a building or an altar. Rashi and Metzudat Zion define it as nitzah, demolition.

Lexically 'he will snatch you up' (the STEPBible sense, from chatah, 'to take up'). The commentators diverge: Rashi reads shevirah, breaking; Meiri reads 'break you', like Jeremiah 1:17, and reports an opinion that it means 'burn you', like Proverbs 25:22; Radak has 'the LORD will take you'. Rare and disputed.
'And he will tear you away', as a plant is torn from the ground; cf. Proverbs 15:25 'the LORD tears down the house of the proud'.

token_glosses.gloss: and he will tear you away

verses.translation_literal: And the righteous will see, and they will fear, and over him they will laugh.
verses.translation_dramatic: The righteous will see it, and they will be afraid; and then, over him, they will laugh.
verses.directors_commentary: Fear and laughter belong together in this line, and the actors should not choose one. Radak and Meiri say the righteous see the revenge and so revere God the more; Rashi says what they say as they laugh is the next verse. The KJV 'The righteous also shall see, and fear, and shall laugh at him' flattens a wordplay: the verb for 'see' (yir'u) and the verb for 'fear' (yira'u) are almost the same sound in Hebrew, one letter apart, so the line is audibly a single chain, seeing becoming fearing. The laughter is not cruel glee; it is the knowing laugh of those who watched a boaster fall (compare Psalm 2:4). 'Over him' (alav) has the sense of 'about him', as in a taunt-song. Keep the laugh short and low, and let the fear come first.

philological_notes.note: A sound play: 'they will see' and 'they will fear', two roots that differ by one letter and are heard almost alike. Metzudat David and Meiri both explain the fear as growing reverence for God.

verses.translation_literal: Look, the man [who] did not make God his refuge, and he trusted in the abundance of his wealth; he took strength in his ruin.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Look at him, the man who would not make God his stronghold, who trusted in the sheer weight of his wealth, and grew strong in his own ruin."
verses.directors_commentary: The laughing righteous now speak, and this is their taunt; Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all take it as the quotation the previous verse promised. 'Look' (hinneh) points at the fallen man; 'the man' (hagever) is Doeg, who has been 'the mighty man' (gibbor) in verse 3, so the title is shrunk to a word for a mere male. The rhetoric is a piece of sound play: ma'uzzo, 'his refuge', and ya'oz, 'he took strength', come from the same root, so the man would not take God as his strength and instead strengthened himself on ruin. Rashi reads the last phrase as 'strengthened himself in his wickedness', which is where the KJV gets its 'wickedness', but hawwah is the word of verse 4, 'ruin', and the repetition matters: what he plotted is what he leaned on. 'The abundance of his wealth' is not a tag, either; Malbim and Metzudat David say he expected Saul to reward him. Deliver it like a proverb quoted over a grave.

philological_notes.note: 'His refuge, his stronghold': a place of strength. It shares the root of ya'oz, 'he became strong', later in the verse. Radak notes the doubled zayin.
'In his ruin' or 'his destruction'; Rashi and Radak take it as 'his wickedness' (rishah, aritzut). The same word as havvot in verse 4.

verses.translation_literal: But I [am] like a luxuriant olive tree in the house of God. I trust in the covenant loyalty of God for ever and ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I, I am an olive tree, green and heavy with leaf, in the house of God. I have put my trust in his faithful love, for ever and ever.
verses.directors_commentary: The camera cuts from the uprooted Doeg to the rooted David, and the contrast is the point of the psalm: 'and I' answers 'the man'. The olive is a tree of long life, one that stays green all year (Radak), that is slow to grow and slow to die; to be one in the 'house of God' is to be planted in a sanctuary, an image of safety. Rashi reads it as children and grandchildren in the house of the LORD, and Ibn Ezra says David is planted there in contrast to Doeg who was 'detained' there (1 Sam 21:8). Malbim notes that an olive is rooted in one place, where Doeg was a stranger in a place he did not belong. The KJV 'green olive tree' gets the colour right but loses ra'anan, which means fresh, juicy, flourishing: the olive is lush, not merely coloured. 'Mercy' for chesed is the KJV's usual softening; it means covenant loyalty, and that is what David's trust leans on. The time frame 'ever and ever' answers 'to perpetuity' in verse 7, because the psalm is built in matching pairs: God's 'forever' undoing, and his 'forever' faithfulness.

philological_notes.note: Luxuriant, fresh, full of sap (Metzudat Zion: 'moist and fresh'). Said of a tree in full leaf (Psalm 92:15, Jeremiah 11:16).
The olive, an evergreen whose leaves do not fall (Radak). A standing image of long life and fruitfulness.

verses.translation_literal: I will give thanks to you for ever, for you have done [it]; and I will wait for your name, for [it is] good, before your faithful ones.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will thank you for ever, because you have done it. And I will wait on your name, for it is good, in the sight of those who are faithful to you.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm closes on gratitude, and the grammar is a little unsteady, so play it as a man catching his breath. 'You have done' is a perfect with no object: Radak and Ibn Ezra say it is the judgment on Doeg; Meiri says the past tense stands for something not yet done, a certainty so strong it speaks in the past (the 'prophetic perfect'). 'Wait for your name' (aqaveh) is a hopeful, stretched waiting, the verb for a rope pulled tight; the KJV 'wait on thy name' makes it sound like service at table. 'Name' stands for God himself, as it does throughout the psalms. The last clause is ambiguous: 'it is good' may describe the name (so KJV and ASV) or the waiting, and 'before' (neged) means 'in front of, in the presence of' your faithful ones (chasidim, the people bound to God by chesed, an echo of the word that has run through the psalm), which the KJV renders 'saints' in its archaic sense. Close quietly, with the faithful gathered around him.

philological_notes.note: 'And I will wait, hope': from a root related to a stretched cord, hence eager, tense waiting. Radak says the form with patach shows the verb is a future.
'Your faithful ones': those who practise chesed, bound to God by it. It echoes chesed El in verse 3 and in verse 10, closing the frame of the psalm.

token_glosses.gloss: I will give thanks to you
